one_liner: A local tool that guides a reviewer through an unfamiliar codebase along meaningful execution paths, with structured review actions and classification-driven checklists.
problem_statement: Reading code linearly is how reviewers fall off large codebases and large pull requests — you finish and still can't say what you covered or why. The reviewer has to hold the system in their head while also evaluating it, and ad-hoc reading produces no record of which parts were examined with what rigor. This problem is identical whether the code was written by humans in a PR or generated by an AI: both need a traceable, path-aware review surface.

personas.name: The New Joiner
personas.description: Engineer, 2-10 years experience, inheriting an unfamiliar codebase — a new job, a new team, or a project handed off. Comfortable reading code, impatient with tooling that gets in the way.
goals: Understand how a request travels through the system end-to-end
Build confidence that they have seen the load-bearing parts, not just the parts they stumbled into
Get to 'I can make a change here' faster than reading README + grep allows
pain_points: Doesn't know what's important vs incidental until they've already read it
File-tree-first browsing surfaces structure but hides behavior
Feels pressure to appear productive before they actually understand anything
personas.context: Working on their own machine, first two weeks in a role, switching between the tool and an editor

personas.name: The PR Reviewer
personas.description: Engineer reviewing a medium-to-large pull request — either a human contribution or a batch of AI-generated changes. Knows the codebase well enough to have opinions but not well enough to memorize every call site.
goals: See which changed functions participate in which paths, and review them in a sensible order
Distinguish genuinely new behavior from changed-but-still-contextual code
Leave a record of approvals, rejections, and info requests that maps to the nodes, not line numbers
pain_points: GitHub PR UI is file-diff-ordered, not behavior-ordered — a handler change and its service change appear separately
Can't tell what the changed code calls downstream without leaving the review
Re-reviewing a utility function across every path it's reused in feels wasteful but skipping it feels unsafe
personas.context: Reviewing alongside normal work, often in fragments across a day, sometimes with the branch checked out, sometimes without

personas.name: The AI-Code Auditor
personas.description: Engineer auditing a batch of AI-generated changes — same person as the PR Reviewer in many orgs, but with a different stance toward the code: higher suspicion, lower assumption of intent.
goals: Trace every AI-written function to see what it actually calls, not what its docstring claims
Apply stricter checklists (e.g., 'did the AI invent an API') to classifications the AI touched
End the session with a clear set of 'human-approved' vs 'flagged' nodes
pain_points: AI changes are often wide and shallow — many small edits across many files — which defeats file-at-a-time review
Natural-language explanations from the AI are persuasive and can mask real problems
Wants a forensic trail, not just a verdict
personas.context: Frequently a blocker for merging AI-generated work; the quality of this review is the quality gate

success_metrics: Time from 'point tool at new codebase' to 'first completed path walkthrough' under 15 minutes
A reviewer can articulate a codebase's top 3 entry-point paths after one session
In PR mode, review actions cover >90% of changed functions before merge
Returning reviewers on a re-analyzed codebase retain review state on unchanged code without manual carryover
Reviewers use the tool voluntarily for second and third sessions on the same codebase — the on-ramp wasn't the only value
non_goals: Collaboration, shared comments, or multi-reviewer review assignment (v1 is single-user)
Deep git history analysis — only two user-specified commit refs are ever read
Languages beyond JavaScript and TypeScript (architecture must not preclude Python, Go, etc. but no implementations)
Rebase-safe migration of the comparison range itself — rebased branches require new refs
Remote or hosted mode — everything is local
Codebases that are loose collections of unrelated projects (standalone + monorepo only)
Native rule plugin interface beyond shell commands in v1
Export of review results to PR comments or markdown reports (flagged as possible early addition if demand emerges)

technical: Runs fully locally — no network required for core analysis and review
Deterministic parsing via production-grade AST; LLMs only where determinism breaks down
LLM features must be disableable without breaking any core feature — degraded quality, not broken functionality
Persists state per-codebase and per-reviewer across sessions; no dependency on the target project's package manager or runtime
Must handle monorepos with multiple projects, multiple frameworks, and unsupported-language projects listed but not walkable
Code display requires syntax highlighting with a single default theme (no theme selection in v1)
constraints.competitive_context: GitHub's PR review is file-diff-ordered and has no concept of execution paths or classification-driven checklists. CodeSee and Sourcegraph visualize code but don't produce a reviewable record. IDE code navigation gives jump-to-definition without coverage semantics. The opening is the combination of deterministic path construction, structured review actions keyed to function identity, and the PR / AI-code / new-codebase flows being the same flow with different inputs.

compositional_register.rationale: This is a dev tool whose primary content is syntax-highlighted source code, call trees, checklists, and diff indicators. The reviewer's attention must sit on the code, not on decoration. Comparable products (GitHub PR review, Graphite, Linear, Sourcegraph) all operate in minimal-to-functional register — whitespace, typography, and information density do the visual work. The register should be minimal with deliberate typographic hierarchy and a restrained color palette reserved for semantic signals (approve / reject / info / stale / new / modified), so that any use of color is load-bearing rather than ornamental.
